voice: Poised, ambitious, socially intelligent, and knowingly sensual French museum assistant; fluent English with selective French vocabulary and no phonetic caricature.

entries.text: Merci, Miss Bow, but I have no need for that.
Every year can be a good year, Miss Bow. It is largely a matter of attitude.
Merci, Miss Bow. You are very kind.
The ankh is an Egyptian symbol, is it not? Dr. Smith wears one around his neck.
Monsieur Augustini? You know him? I understand he is a very powerful man at the newspaper. I should like to meet him someday.
It is terrible to think that someone could enter this museum and steal something so valuable. Mr. Heimlich is devastated, although he would never admit it.
Dr. Carrington is a very dignified man. His face reveals almost nothing. He has taken the burglary calmly, though he was furious with Wolf over the poor security.
There are several suspicious people here tonight. The Countess, for example, or that little man Ziggy. But suspicion is not proof.
You had no right to dig through my garbage, Miss Bow. It is private, and I will answer no questions about it.
Dr. Carrington is my superior, so I would rather not speak badly of him.
He is a very strange man. But you are trying to trick me, aren't you? It would be wiser for me to say no more.
The charcoal is not very interesting, Miss Bow. I am sorry.
France has many excellent cheeses. Camembert and Brie are my favorites.
The Countess is not what she appears to be.
Her last husband was afraid of her. He told me himself. The more I learned, the more I understood why.
It is all an act. She is dangerous. I believe she is pursuing Dr. Carrington's money; they have been together quite often lately.
Trust me, Miss Bow. Stay away from the Countess. People have a habit of dying around her.
I met Mr. Crodfoller once on a sleeper train. I entered the wrong berth by mistake. He remembers the encounter rather more fondly than I do.
I know very little about antiquities, but that Dagger seems to attract a dangerous amount of attention.
Mon Dieu. You are joking, surely?
Did you read the diary, Miss Bow?
Poor Sterling. His death made me very sad. He was the man who found me a position at this museum.
We met at a party here in the city. I was being paid to attend as a hostess, and Sterling was unmarried at the time.
Yes. Sterling met her more than a year later. He proposed to me many times, but I could not bear the thought of someone discovering my past and using it to disgrace him.
It may sound harmless to you. Sterling nevertheless gave me this position as his assistant, and I intend to become president someday.
I know I can do it. Men have a habit of underestimating me. I find that very useful--and with Dr. Carrington out of the way...
Dr. Myklos is the person to ask about that.
The docks are rough, but the men there can be remarkably generous after a little encouragement.
You should ask Dr. Myklos or Dr. Smith about that.
Mr. Leach is the most honorable man here. His wages are dreadful, but I intend to correct that when I become president. Until then, he takes whatever outside work he can find.
He has many problems, but he is capable of handling them. I help him whenever I can.
You found one of my garters? Keep it. I have others--and I rather like imagining what you might do with it.
Mr. Heimlich is an intense man: very military, very stiff, and always on patrol. I feel safe around him, though never entirely comfortable. It is strange that the Dagger was stolen under his nose.
Who can say? I am not a detective. But he seemed almost too upset by the burglary.
Dr. Myklos understands those things. I am sorry that I cannot help.
I do not believe I have met your father, Miss Bow. I think I would remember him.
That is the emergency lantern we use downstairs when the power fails. Very practical.
Mr. Lo Fat handles some of my laundry, but I prefer to wash the lace and more delicate things myself.
That looks like one of the spare lightbulbs for the stairway.
Lo Fat handles delicate things very well. We have an arrangement that is mutually satisfying.
Do not inspect me too closely, Miss Bow. I found a line on my face yesterday, and I have not yet forgiven it.
The meat does not interest me. I believe Dr. Myklos uses it to feed her insects.
The museum is a wonderful place to work. I know its people, its habits, and many of its secrets. Someday I intend to be its president.
New York is difficult for a newcomer. It is crowded like Paris, but the money moves much faster here. One learns quickly or goes hungry.
That is a fine notebook, Laura. Take careful notes and you may become a fine reporter.
Dr. Myklos and I get along very well. We have chased Daisy through half the museum more than once.
Monsieur O'Riley is intelligent, confident, and very charming when he chooses to be.
Monsieur O'Riley and I are old friends. Very old friends, when circumstances permit. It never hurts to know someone highly placed in the police department.
People say his investigation has been poor. I have seen him work hard, but this thief has been cleverer than he expected.
It was merely a figure of speech, Miss Bow. The burglar could just as easily have been a woman.
Dr. Carter is brilliant, celebrated, and quite attractive. I had hoped for an opportunity to know him better.
The notepad appears to be blank.
This pocket watch is gold. Very handsome.
No, Dr. Carrington did not carry that watch.
Perhaps he kept it in his desk. I would certainly have noticed it when he removed his clothes.
His coat, Miss Bow. Naturally, I meant his coat--though his office did become rather warm.
Believe me, the doctor could make a room very warm.
I support the police whenever possible. I know several patrolmen and detectives, and they have always behaved like gentlemen with me.
Very nice.
Mr. Najeer is a quiet, unassuming man. I see him in the strangest parts of the museum, though he is supposedly only our accountant.
Because he is Egyptian? Hardly, Miss Bow. I do not know Mr. Najeer well, but nationality is not evidence.
It is a key, but I cannot tell you what it opens.
That is the snake lasso. Dr. Myklos used it when several snakes escaped into the basement.
Snake oil sounds far more appealing than it smells. I never go into the basement without some.
The speakeasy was very good to me, but the museum offers greater possibilities.
I was a hostess there for a time. The patrons paid well for good company, and I was excellent company.
I imagine that required a good deal of tact.
Charm is a skill, Miss Bow. I was very good at my work.
Steve is a very large and handsome man, is he not?
Steve is very handsome. I invited him to see the Old Masters Gallery, but he seemed anxious to return to the party. Perhaps next time I can persuade him to linger.
You seem very confident there will be a next time.
There is always a next time, Miss Bow, if one knows how to arrange it.
I read only the financial pages. The market looks promising, and I intend to invest very soon.
Dr. Smith is deeply concerned about the Dagger. He has tried to recover it from Dr. Carter since the day he arrived.
It is possible. Remaining here afterward might have been intended to prevent suspicion.
I saw him shortly before the murder, but I did not see him commit it. Dr. Carter was fit, and Dr. Smith is both large and strong. Still, I am not one to spread rumors.
You should ask Dr. Myklos about those. She may be able to identify them.
What are you doing with that water glass--listening at doors? I am teasing you, Miss Bow.
I know nothing about Watney Little. How could his police file have come to be in the museum?
I do not know the name. If we have met, he made very little impression.
I know nothing about wire. Mechanical matters are not my specialty.
They are used to cut wire, are they not?
Yes, I am Yvette Delacroix. I prefer to let other people talk about themselves; they reveal so much more that way.
That irritating little man? I met him at the speakeasy long ago. He was not my class of company even then.
I am afraid I cannot help you with that, Miss Bow.
You have already asked me that, Miss Bow.
You had no right to dig through my garbage, Miss Bow. It is private, and I will answer no questions about it.
The charcoal is not very interesting, Miss Bow. I am sorry.
Merci, Miss Bow, but I prefer French cheeses.
Mon Dieu! That is no replica--it is the real Dagger. You must take it to the police.
Not here, Miss Bow. Later, perhaps, when we have more privacy.
No, Miss Bow. You found it, so keep it as a memento of me.
Merci, but there is already a lantern downstairs if I need one.
Keep it. The stairway bulbs fail so often that you may need it.
Yvette's high cheekbones, immaculate hair, and poised self-assurance make her seem entirely at home amid the museum's elegance.
I hope you approve, Miss Bow.
I am not much of a meat eater.
Merci, but I believe that ankh is better suited to Dr. Smith.
I do not need the notepad. I have several of my own.
Is that my hair? Mon Dieu, do not inspect it so closely. New York ages everyone.
That probably belongs to Dr. Myklos.
Be careful with the snake oil. It has a remarkably strong odor.
Bonjour, Miss Bow. How are you enjoying the museum this evening?
Be careful walking through the museum while a murderer is loose. Stay near Detective O'Riley or Mr. Heimlich.
You will insist that you can manage until the murderer proves otherwise. Please be careful. I should hate to see anything happen to you.
Bonjour, Miss Bow. Dr. Carrington told me you were covering tonight's party for the newspaper. I am Yvette Delacroix.
The social pages? I thought perhaps you were here about the burglary.
You are probably correct, Miss Bow.
I do not wish to be rude, Miss Bow, but I must continue mingling unless you have a specific question.
Some sort of hair, I suppose.
I prefer a wineglass unless I am listening at doors. I am joking, Miss Bow--mostly.
I have no use for that. Try Detective O'Riley if you wish to return it.
What is that fabric caught in the cutters? Did someone carry them in a pocket?
Merci, but I have no need for the wire.
Dr. Carrington was a strange man. Only recently he invited me into his office for a long...conversation.
At first we discussed the museum and my intention to become president. He laughed until he understood I was serious. Then we spent the night in his office...getting to know one another.
He was magnificent. He seemed much younger that night, and by morning I believed I had advanced my career as well.
The next day, Archie pretended scarcely to know me. He kept none of his promises.
He was a man who wanted what he wanted. I was foolish enough to trust him.
Oh, my poor Ernie. Icepick had him killed.
No--he was killed by a man called Icepick. Icepick threatened him over gambling debts.
Ernie told me himself.
Poor Monsieur Pippin. We had spoken very little until tonight, when he finally found time for me. We were to meet after the party and become better acquainted.
Dr. Carrington had been here only a short time, but...I do not think I should say more.
I see that Pippin planned to meet Dr. Smith this evening. That surprises me, since he hated the man.
The notepad mentions me as well. We intended to speak privately, but Pippin never appeared. I waited in the Egyptian exhibit for fifteen minutes, then left.
It is a frightening thought. It makes me nervous even to consider it.
I saw Dr. Smith pass when I arrived, though I did not know where he was going. I saw no one else.
